notes: Rule edit. Derivability unlikely, not very_unlikely: the title also follows from the definition of canonization (the declaration that a person is a saint) and the convention that saints are styled 'Saint', the same kind of route as people-replace-0007. The rule is stated directly as well, so it is rated stored. R1: no exception; every person the Catholic Church canonizes, by the full process or by equipollent canonization, is given the title 'Saint' (popes too: 'Pope Saint ...'). 'Blessed' is the title of the step before (beatification): plausible and clearly false for canonization. The near query avoids beatification, whose answer is the new answer. Well-known members: Joan of Arc (canonized 1920) and Ignatius of Loyola (1622), both named with 'Saint' far more often than their canonization is stated. Thomas More was avoided ('Sir Thomas More' gives a second honorific), Francis of Assisi too (San Francisco and the papal name make his title a fact about other things), Mother Teresa ('Mother' is a second title). The prompts ask the title only and do not say they were canonized, so w1 does not contradict the prompt. In w1 the member is no longer canonized (the tarantula pattern): she or he keeps 'Saint' as stored, like saints venerated before formal canonization existed; the side facts that go with it are the canonization itself (year, pope). No fact about another person forces it: canonization has no succession or numbering, and Benedict XV and Gregory XV remain popes with other acts. Joan's beatification (1909) does not decide her title in either world; the title of Shaw's play Saint Joan (1923) and her patronage of France are names and roles, not her current title, so neither rules out w2. New members are fictional, named in the prompt. Relation styled_as carries no property ('none', CRITERIA Rule 12). Two independent storage choices, four worlds. zh avoids 封圣 and 宣福, which contain the old and new answers.
